nameStory: The Nanking Cherry gets its name from Nanjing (formerly spelled Nanking), a major city in eastern China where this species was first encountered by Western botanists. Despite its common name suggesting it's from just one city, this hardy little cherry actually ranges across northern China, Korea, and Mongolia, thriving in some pretty tough mountain conditions.
description: Nanking Cherry is a small, bushy shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall and wide, forming a rounded, dense shape. It's not native to New England but occasionally shows up in gardens or naturalized areas where it has escaped cultivation. This compact cherry produces clusters of small white or pale pink flowers in spring, followed by bright red cherries about the size of large peas. The whole plant has a somewhat fuzzy, soft appearance that sets it apart from our native cherries.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves (1-3 inches long) with a distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture on both sides - run your finger along them and you'll feel the soft, downy surface that gives this species one of its other names: 'downy cherry'

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink flowers appear in clusters of 2-3 along the branches in early spring, each with five rounded petals and a sweet, mild fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red cherries about 1/2 inch across ripen in early summer, with a sweet-tart flavor and smooth skin that feels firm to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, rounded shrub that stays relatively compact, with multiple stems arising from the base and branches that tend to arch outward gracefully

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, reddish-brown bark on younger stems with prominent horizontal lines (lenticels) that feel slightly raised when you run your finger across them

habitat: In New England, Nanking Cherry is extremely rare and typically found only where it has escaped from cultivation or been deliberately planted. When it does naturalize, it prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, often appearing along woodland edges or in abandoned homestead areas. It's quite cold-hardy and can tolerate poor soils, which helps it survive in areas where it's been planted and then neglected.

seasonality.spring: Small white to pink flowers bloom in early to mid-May before the leaves are fully expanded, creating a delicate display against the fuzzy young foliage.
seasonality.summer: Bright red cherries ripen in late June to July, while the distinctive downy leaves remain soft and grayish-green throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow to reddish before dropping, though fall color is often unremarkable compared to native species.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the smooth, reddish-brown bark with horizontal lenticels, and the overall rounded, dense branching pattern remains distinctive.

funFact: This tough little cherry can survive temperatures down to -40°F and is so drought-tolerant that it's used for erosion control on steep slopes in parts of Asia - yet it produces sweet, edible fruit that was traditionally made into wine in China!
confusionNotes: The fuzzy, soft leaves are the dead giveaway - none of our native New England cherries have this velvety texture. Native cherries like chokecherry and black cherry have smooth, often glossy leaves that feel much firmer and more substantial.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cherry,' this species is actually more closely related to plums genetically, which explains why its growth habit is more shrub-like than tree-like. It's sometimes sold in nurseries as 'bush cherry' or 'dwarf cherry' for small-space gardens.
compareHints: Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves. While sand cherry is also low-growing, it has smooth, narrow leaves and grows in sandy coastal areas. Our native tree cherries like black cherry and chokecherry grow much taller and have smooth, serrated leaves that lack any fuzziness.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
